what_its_for: Brentuximab vedotin is a cancer medicine used to treat certain types of lymphoma (cancer of the lymph system). It is used for Hodgkin lymphoma and a type called systemic anaplastic large cell lymphoma (sALCL), as well as some other CD30-positive lymphomas. It works by targeting and killing cancer cells that have a specific protein called CD30 on their surface.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it is delivered directly into your vein through a needle or catheter. A nurse or doctor will give it to you in a clinic or hospital setting. Each infusion usually takes about 30 minutes. You will NOT give this medicine to yourself at home. Always tell your care team if you feel any discomfort, burning, or unusual sensations during the infusion.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your body weight. The usual dose is 1.8 mg per kilogram of body weight, given once every 3 weeks. Your doctor may adjust your dose or pause your treatment depending on how your body responds or if you experience side effects. Never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given by a healthcare professional in a clinic, it is very important to keep all of your scheduled appointments. If you miss or need to reschedule an appointment, call your doctor or care team as soon as possible to set up a new time. Do not try to double up on doses.
storage: You do not need to store this medicine at home. It is prepared and stored by healthcare professionals at the clinic or hospital. If you are ever given any supplies related to your treatment, keep them in a secure place out of reach of children and pets, and follow any specific storage instructions provided by your care team.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol or taking medications that can harm your liver or kidneys without checking with your doctor first. Do not receive live vaccines (such as the shingles vaccine Zostavax or the nasal flu vaccine) while being treated with this medicine, as they could be dangerous for you. Avoid close contact with people who are sick, since your immune system may be weakened. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after your last dose if you are a woman, or for at least 6 months after if you are a man, because this medicine can harm an unborn baby. Avoid breastfeeding during treatment and for at least 3 months after your last dose.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: numbness, tingling, or weakness in your hands or feet (nerve problems); fever of 100.4°F or higher, chills, or signs of infection; shortness of breath, chest pain, or a new cough; severe stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea; yellowing of your skin or eyes, or dark urine (liver problems); unusual bruising or bleeding; a skin rash, blistering, or peeling skin; swelling of your face, lips, or throat during or after the infusion; confusion, memory problems, or changes in your vision or speech; or any new or worsening symptoms that concern you.
when_it_works: Your doctor will monitor your response to treatment through regular check-ups, blood tests, and imaging scans (such as PET or CT scans). Some patients begin to see a response after a few treatment cycles, but it may take several weeks or months to see the full benefit. Every patient is different, so stay in close communication with your care team about how your treatment is going.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: This medicine can cause serious harm to an unborn baby. Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. Do not breastfeed during treatment. Children: Brentuximab vedotin has been approved for use in some children and teenagers with certain types of lymphoma. The dose will be carefully calculated based on the child's weight by their doctor. Older adults (65 and over): Older adults may have a higher risk of certain side effects. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Kidney or liver problems: If you have kidney or liver disease, your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more carefully.
